textRun.content: The goal of this document is to close the understanding gap between product + engineering, and Steve. It is meant to be a starting point that makes it easy for people to pile on questions, get answers asynchronously, and build shared understanding quickly.

The intended behavior is curiosity before certainty. When something is unclear or people have different perspectives, start by asking how the product or strategy is intended to work and use the answer to build shared understanding. Questions and dialogue help us surface context, align on what is current, and identify opportunities to improve. The goal is to make it easy for people to ask, learn, and contribute, while treating this document as a living starting point rather than unquestionable truth.

This tab consolidates the current answers and supporting context. It keeps a distinction between current goals, directional hypotheses, and questions that are intentionally still open, so the document can be updated as shared understanding improves.

The most existential goal is product-led growth, specifically solving the top of the funnel and creating sustained, non-linear growth. The desired system is self-feeding: one person uses or shares an Agent-Native template or application, that brings more people into the experience, those people customize or use it, and their sharing or successful outcomes attract still more users.

The immediate priority is therefore template adoption and user success, not producing a large number of templates. The strategy is to have fewer, stronger templates and applications that people actually use, share, clone, and return to. Once people are successfully using a template, Builder and Fusion can give them good paths to customize, enhance, or build on that experience (as well as build net-new apps from shared pieces).

1. Product-led growth and template adoption are first. We need evidence that people are entering the templates, succeeding, sharing them, and creating a self-reinforcing user base. Growth at the top of the funnel is the highest priority.

2. Developer adoption is second. NPM downloads, GitHub stars, framework usage, and developer interest are important positive signals, although they are harder to directly influence and instrument than template usage.

3. Enterprise is third in the prioritization order, not because it is unimportant, but because the top of the funnel is more critical to achieve faster growth than you can with a pure top-down sales approach. But it’s critical we spend at least ~20% of our time here making sure we are building core things deals need (and unblocking deals) remains important with such a top-down heavy company to date.

Product-led growth is working when the set of repeat users to Agent-Native users is growing (as rapidly as possible). Clips is an example of the self-feeding loop: people create and share clips, other people join to watch or use them, and that creates more usage and distribution.
Developer adoption is visible through npm package downloads and GitHub stars. These signals are valuable but less directly controllable than template adoption.

Enterprise progress is measured by our ability to progress deals - make sure we have the pieces that make for a pitch that prospects find to be intriguing and differentiated, POV success rate, and ultimately closing deals at a reasonable rate (noting it will tend to be low at first and the goal is to make it rise). It is not measured by accumulating a huge enterprise feature list.

The default allocation should be approximately 70-80 percent toward product-led growth and 20-30 percent toward enterprise needs, with the exact split remaining flexible as evidence changes. Most of the PLG investment is on the template and application side: make the example apps work well, in doing so improve the framework, and make the first-touch experience great across the board (example apps as well as building with the framework in Builder or other tools).

When self-serve and enterprise needs diverge, the shared 80 to 90 percent should win first. Both groups fundamentally need to make useful applications reliably, with clean onboarding, a strong starting point, understandable application behavior, and good workspace capabilities. Divergent enterprise requirements should be evaluated based on deal value, frequency, strategic leverage, and whether the capability also creates a self-serve win.

Explicit deferrals include adding a giant enterprise feature set, creating more templates simply to increase the catalog, making Workspaces a mandatory gate for everyone, or treating Factory as a large Zapier or n8n replacement before validating the actual workflows.

The product is still a horizontal framework, but we should simultaneously probe for the fastest-growing use cases and the users who adopt the fastest. Horizontal platform breadth and focused use-case depth are not opposites: the framework stays general while product investment follows evidence of traction.

Product and engineering teams are a strong initial hypothesis because Builder already has relationships and an existing audience there. Their needs are also generalizable: requirements, feedback, triage, PRDs, RFCs, design, implementation, and workflows that connect applications and agents. Go-to-market teams are another major opportunity, especially because there are internal use cases around pipeline, customer, sales, marketing, and QBR workflows and where we’ve seen the most internal traction around Agent-Native (and previously Fusion apps) interest and usage.
We are in a learning phase
. We should watch which example apps grow fastest, which personas use them, where users achieve outcomes, and which workflows generate organic sharing.

Individuals, enterprise teams, and functional teams all need the same basics: ask for what they want, receive a useful application reliably, understand what the agent can do, use the application successfully, and have a clear path to customize or extend it. This shared core is where most product and engineering investment should go.

Out of scope for now are assumptions that we are replacing every specialist tool, solving every enterprise administration request, choosing one permanent first persona, or fully specifying every workspace and Factory workflow before observing real use.

There are two related creation paths. Developers should be able to use the open-source framework from the CLI with their own coding agent. Less technical or more product-oriented users should be able to prompt in Fusion (soon called “Builder Code”). The underlying needs are similar: the person describes an outcome, the agent creates a useful app, and the user can inspect, use, customize, and deploy it.

The first prompt experience should not force users to understand any Agent-Native vocabulary up front. The system should infer whether they want a pure chat experience, an application with a UI, a full agentic application with tools, or some combination. It should ask focused follow-up questions when needed and make those choices discoverable from the prompt.

The default path should be simple and app-level, similar to the simplicity of a Lovable-style experience. A user should not need to understand Workspaces, monorepos, branches, or governance before making a successful first app. They should be able to adopt those capabilities later when the complexity becomes useful.

The end-to-end loop is: describe the desired outcome, generate the app and its agent surface, try it, share or deploy it, observe real use, then customize or extend it in Builder. The quality of the first-touch guidance and the reliability of the generated result are more important than exposing every advanced option.

First, a monorepo structure: all of the applications/agents live in one repository, which means they can share code, constraints, components, credentials, and other governed resources. A change or constraint can be managed centrally rather than duplicated across unrelated projects.

Second, governance: applications and agents can move through the organization's own CI systems, approval gates, access controls, and review processes. Dispatch is the administrative surface for deciding who can use which applications, who can use which keys, which applications can use which keys, who has access to what, what is connected, and what is being used.

Dispatch should also support visibility into usage, costs, monitoring, audit trails, and rollout metrics across the Agent-Native ecosystem. It is the general administrative interface, not merely a settings page for one app.

Standalone apps should eventually be able to move into a workspace, although migration is not trivial and could be slow or fail if handled poorly. The product should not require people to make the workspace decision before they understand the value. The migration path is strategically important even if the first implementation is incremental.

Hosting and deployment of workspaces are simpler than people likely assume. A workspace deploys as one unit, with each application available at a path under the workspace root. The existing deployment model supports one database by default, with multiple databases as an option, and existing hosting and database providers such as Netlify and Neon are intended to work without a separate infrastructure setup for every application. Aka the same way we do hosting and neon for one app (standard build and netlify deploy, single DATABASE_URL for Neon) works at the workspace level too with no additional setup.

Important product seams include the app-to-workspace migration path, clear branch and repository semantics, a non-confusing project versus workspace model, governance and Dispatch integration, and the ability to run background tasks so slow checks or long agent work do not block the next action.

Workspaces should not be an automatic self-serve gate. The default individual experience can remain app-first and simple. An enterprise POV or known enterprise deployment can start with a workspace because the organization will almost certainly need shared governance, access control, auditability, and centralized management.

That does not mean enterprise is the only audience for Workspaces. A self-serve user may later want to combine apps, share resources, or move from a single app into a governed workspace. The product should make that transition understandable and technically possible.

The minimum enterprise layer is mostly shared framework functionality: who can use which apps, who can use which credentials, which agents are connected, what is being used, costs, audit logs, monitoring, CI, approvals, and basic administration. Most of this exists in Agent-Native Dispatch today. These should be connected cleanly to Fusion rather than recreated as a huge separate feature set.

An MVP can unblock workspace usage without a complete UI overhaul. People can already use a repository-like structure, create branches, edit multiple apps, and create new apps by prompting. The next step is to repair the obviously confusing parts, make the existing flow legible, and learn from customer use before committing to a comprehensive redesign.

Workspace UX improvements should be, to an extent, incremental. Improve the current project and branch surfaces, make workspace state discoverable, add the most important governance and admin connections, and keep the simple standalone app path intact. A full first-class overhaul should follow actual customer and internal feedback rather than precede it.

There are not yet hard dates that GTM should communicate. The safe commitment is directional: individual app creation is the immediate release, then improvements to the first-touch creation experience being improved, then Workspaces as a first-class construct in Builder.
Current task is to plan these features out more thoroughly and set target dates accordingly.

Factory is a thin coordination layer for Agent-Native apps and agents. It lets people arrange existing apps into precise, visible multi-step workflows, while existing automation infrastructure provides execution and run history. Unlike n8n or Zapier, its nodes are Agent-Native apps with their own tools and integrations. The first wedge remains open: validate product, GTM, and enterprise workflows through dogfooding and targeted customer use, looking for repeat creation, sharing, successful runs, and deal value before expanding the MVP.

The market hypothesis is that Builder can provide a horizontal Agent-Native framework while using high-growth applications and templates as the product-led entry points. We should invest in depth where we see traction and retain breadth in the underlying framework.

Relatively fixed principles are the shared app and agent model, the importance of reliable first-touch creation, the value of specialized apps that can work together, the need for a simple self-serve path, and the priority of outcomes and adoption over raw construction volume.

Open decisions include the fastest-growing use cases, the first persona wedge, how much Workspaces should be exposed by default, the exact Dispatch UX, the best Factory insertion point, and which app surfaces create the most viral distribution.

Evidence to double down includes repeat use, fast cloning, organic sharing, successful outcomes, strong retention, and enterprise demand that maps to the shared core. Evidence to change direction includes weak adoption, no sharing or repeat use, high implementation cost for low value, or recurring feedback that the chosen surface does not solve a real problem. Evidence to stop includes a lack of use and a lack of feedback after a fair test, especially when the feature is expensive or confusing.
12. Goals, capabilities, and non-goals of the key Agent-Native app/template experiences
The overall goals for the example apps is two-fold:
Create and test opportunities to give people a clear and prescriptive first-touch with the Agent-Native framework that has a potential to lead to exponential growth through WoM and sharing
Battle test the framework and improve it
Build out the toolkit of reusable pieces people can use in their apps (chat, notion-like editing, etc)

There’s a lot of scope here and the intention is to focus on those that have the biggest measured impact from real world use. The goal is to not add more templates but to focus where we see heat and traction.

These entries below describe the intended job of each app, the capabilities that make it valuable, and the boundaries that keep it focused. The apps are different faces of a shared Agent-Native system: they should be able to use shared actions, data, state, context, assets, and governance, while still having a clear job for the person using them.

Goal: Be a reliable, low-friction drop-in replacement for Loom. The core experience is recording a useful clip, sharing it, and making it easy for another person to watch, understand, and act on it. The value is not only the recording itself; it is the distribution loop created when clips are shared with people who then enter the product and use it.

Core value and capabilities: Clips should make capture, sharing, playback, and lightweight context feel dependable. We currently also explore adjacent workflows such as meeting recording and Whisper-style transcription, but those are secondary to the core clip loop. A strong clip experience is valuable both as a standalone utility and as a product-led entry point that creates more users through sharing.

Non-goals: Clips should not keep expanding every recording experiment indefinitely. Secondary workflows need real usage and actionable feedback to earn continued investment. High complexity with low usage, or no usage and no feedback after a fair test, is a signal to simplify, deprecate, or stop investing.
Status: nearing completion, launch coming soon

Goal: Standardize high-quality, on-brand decks for repeatable workflows such as QBRs, first meetings, customer context, and internal presentations. The outcome is a deck that has the right story, customer or business context, instructions, visual system, and assets without every person rebuilding the process from scratch.

Core value and capabilities: Slides should combine specialized Agent-Native capabilities rather than act as an isolated deck editor. Analytics can supply the relevant data and interpretation, Assets can supply approved images or other media, and users should be able to import and export to other common deck building tools like.ppt and google slides. The system should support reusable workflows and templates so teams can produce consistent decks that are accurate, on-brand, and appropriate to the audience.

Non-goals: Slides is not merely a generic presentation editor, and the goal is not for every team to build a disconnected deck generator. It should not preserve a world where everyone makes separate, off-brand decks with duplicated instructions and data connections. The product should own the reusable, connected workflow while still producing ordinary shareable presentations.

Goal: Help non-technical teammates, especially go-to-market teams, answer bounded ad hoc customer, product, and business questions without learning the underlying data tools. The experience should find the relevant source or sources, apply known definitions and filters, and return an understandable answer with enough context to judge its reliability.

Focused capabilities: When a question genuinely requires it, Analytics may combine a small number of relevant sources such as HubSpot, product analytics, Gong, session data, or BigQuery, and produce a simple chart or reusable view. Definitions, source ownership, caveats, and provenance should be visible. Agent-to-agent access and connections to apps such as Slides are useful extensions, but they do not expand the MVP into an all-purpose data platform.

Analytics is not a replacement for Amplitude, Sigma, BI tools, data warehouses, or expert analysts. It is not a comprehensive reporting suite, generic dashboard builder, or mandate to recreate every existing report and integration.

Analytics is not meant to answer every possible business question, onboard every data source at once, or make every teammate a data engineer. It should not be a black box that hides metric definitions, source limitations, or how a result was produced. Deep exploratory analysis, governed enterprise reporting, and specialized workflows remain with the expert tools and teams that already own them.

The default Postgres database can support an MVP and smaller datasets, but it is not the permanent analytics warehouse at scale. Larger deployments should connect an appropriate analytical backend such as BigQuery. Analytics also does not own every downstream workflow; other apps should consume its outputs through clear contracts rather than pulling the entire data stack into Analytics.
Goal: Provide a Figma-like design interface over real application code, especially for designers and builder personas close to Builder's ICP.
Core value and capabilities: Design should allow visual generation and editing as plain HTML, and ultimately connect Builder to build and deploy full React applications. More info

Non-goals: Design is not intended to be a generic design tool detached from running applications or a place to produce mocks that have no path to implementation. It is not a replacement for Figma.
Status: in development, early dogfooding, launch coming soon

Goal: Be a Notion-like, AI-driven starting point for information, artifacts, text, and written content. People should be able to import or create documents, ask agents to find and use relevant context, and create new material from that context.

Core value and capabilities: Content should make the editor and document primitives useful to both people and agents. The document surface can become reusable toolkit infrastructure for other apps that need rich text, structured content, collaboration, or generated artifacts. The strongest version of Content combines a good authoring experience with retrieval, context, and agent actions rather than treating the editor as a passive storage surface.

Non-goals: Content is not merely a document editor with no agent context. It should not become a silo that duplicates Brain, source evidence, or every other app's specialized workflow. The likely direction is a stronger shared knowledge and content hub, potentially combining or renaming the Brain and Content boundaries instead of maintaining two overlapping products.
Status: in development, early dogfooding. Likely will be deleted and merged into Content app

Goal: Provide a central company knowledge repository that can use current information from Slack, Granola, and other connected sources while respecting sensitivity, sanitization, auditability, provenance, and visibility into what people ask.

Core value and capabilities: Brain should make knowledge useful to both humans and agents. It should help people find the current answer, show where an answer came from, preserve access and sensitivity boundaries, and make the organization’s accumulated context available to other Agent-Native apps. Provenance, evidence quality, freshness, and visibility into usage are part of the product value, not implementation details. Brain should also provide a path for important, reviewed knowledge to be preferentially retrieved rather than leaving every answer dependent on an unstructured search.

Non-goals: Brain should not be a thin, isolated answer bot that produces confident unsourced claims. It should not silently use stale or sensitive material, hide the evidence behind an answer, or treat access controls and audit history as optional. It likely should not remain a separate product boundary from Content if both are serving the same knowledge, document, and context needs.

Goal: Coordinate multiple Agent-Native agents or apps into a simple, visible, precise workflow. Factory should let one agent or app supply context or a result to another, combine steps, and expose the run state and history.

Core value and capabilities: Factory is a thin coordination and control layer over existing Agent-Native apps, agents, and automation primitives. It can support sequential steps, conditional logic, multiple agent touches, reusable flows, run logs, and status visibility. Existing automation infrastructure should provide the execution and history where possible instead of Factory inventing a separate execution model.

Non-goals: Factory is not an n8n, Zapier, or generic integration-marketplace replacement. It is not a commitment to a large standalone product, a universal catalog of workflow nodes, or arbitrary integrations before the actual Agent-Native use cases are understood. It should not become a large platform before dogfooding and customer evidence show which workflows are valuable.

Goal: Generate on-brand images, and secondarily video, with the right brand and content context. Assets should become a shared digital asset manager and generation capability that Design, Slides, Content, and other agents can use.

Core value and capabilities: The value is shared brand context, approved or reusable assets, and consistent generation instructions. Other apps should be able to request the right asset through a common capability instead of each app implementing its own generation prompts, brand rules, and asset handling.

Non-goals: Do not maintain separate image-generation implementations and instructions in every app. Assets is not only a one-off image generator; the shared context, reuse, and integration surface are the strategic value.
Goal: Provide a simple, useful form workflow for internal needs. Forms is a focused utility that can be created, used, and extended without requiring a large product surface.

Core value and capabilities: The app should cover straightforward collection and submission flows and can serve as a small example of an Agent-Native utility with a useful UI and agent-accessible actions.
Non-goals: Forms is not currently a major investment or strategic focus. It should not accumulate a broad form-builder roadmap unless usage and feedback create a clear reason to invest.
Status: complete, solid traction. No ongoing work

Goal: Help people plan and recap work in a visual, shareable way. The experience has meaningful usage and some viral potential because plans and recaps can be shared as artifacts rather than remaining inside a private chat.

Core value and capabilities: Plan should make complex work easier to understand through visual plans, recaps, and structured artifacts that people can inspect and discuss. It also demonstrates the value of an Agent-Native app that turns a conversation or work history into a useful, durable visual output.

Non-goals: Plan and Visual Plan is not the largest current investment area because it generally works and has produced less actionable feedback or clear growth opportunity than surfaces such as Clips. It should continue to improve where evidence supports it without taking priority away from stronger adoption loops.
Status: complete. Small fixes as they arise.

Goal: Serve as the basic starter surface and a simple place to begin an Agent-Native app experience. Chat gives a user an approachable entry point for describing a need and discovering what an agent or application can do.

Core value and capabilities: Chat can help a person move from an initial request toward a useful app, workflow, or answer. It is a simple front door, but it should connect to the broader system of applications, tools, data, state, and shared actions.

Non-goals: Chat alone is not the whole Agent-Native product and is not the destination for every workflow. The framework is about useful applications, agents, shared actions, data, state, context, and specialized faces, not raw chat volume or a single universal conversation surface.

The common product is not a collection of unrelated apps. Each app should have a clear user-facing job while participating in a shared system where agents can call one another and reuse actions, data, state, context, assets, and governance. For example, Analytics can supply grounded data to Slides, Assets can supply on-brand media to Slides and Design, Content and Brain can provide shared knowledge, and Factory can coordinate multi-step flows across these capabilities.
Do not optimize for creating more templates as an end in itself. Build fewer strong entry points and make their usage grow.

Do not assume Agent-Native means replacing every existing specialist tool. Analytics complements expert tools, Slides complements existing deck workflows, and the apps should use the right connected systems.
Do not turn Factory into a generic Zapier or n8n alternative before understanding the Agent-Native orchestration use cases.
Do not add a massive enterprise feature list when most enterprise and self-serve needs overlap.
Do not force every self-serve user into Workspaces before the value is clear.
Do not lock down the first persona, Factory use case, or complete workspace UX before customer and dogfooding evidence.
Do not let confident assumptions replace questions, source-backed answers, and explicit discussion of what is still unknown.

Can I edit an existing AN template as a non-dev? ie on Builder.

Yes. Customers should be able to choose an Agent Native template as a starting point inside Builder and edit it without being a developer. The framework already supports creating from a template; the missing piece is a simple Builder flow for selecting a template and starting a project from it.

Internal employees can edit the root templates in the Agent Native project, but those shared starting points need a high quality bar and clear ownership because changes affect everyone who uses them. For customers, the intended workflow is to start from a trusted template and customize it to fit their own needs.

What kind of apps do we expect users (self-serve and Enterprise) to be building? Do we expect them to edit AN templates to suit their needs, build internal tools, or just simply create AI-supported apps for public use? I understand that it’s likely a mix, but what do we want, and who are we building for?

We should not decide on one persona or use case before validating where the strongest pull is. Agent Native is horizontal, so the plan is to test the market and adjust based on real customer and user learning.

The primary near-term hypothesis is internal tools and knowledge-work apps. A particularly strong starting point is turning work done by AI power users into an app that everyone else can repeat, such as generating a QBR deck, PRD, RFC, analytics result, or other repeatable workflow. Templates for analytics, slides, content, design, and related capabilities can provide a useful starting point and reusable building blocks for larger agent workflows.

Net-new public or consumer-facing apps are also possible, but they are a more distant third priority. The immediate goal is to give organizations a way to package expertise, make it accessible to more people, and learn which workflows have the strongest demand.

Do you have examples of the kind of edits people have made to existing AN templates? Given that we’ve added so much to (for example) the Clips app, what’s really left for other people to add? Or are these people using the template as just a part of a larger app?

Clips is not the best example of the intended pattern. It has been a useful experiment for awareness and customization, but the feedback so far has mostly been to make it work consistently, correctly, and performantly, with feature parity to Loom. It is not the archetypal app that we expect customers to fork and substantially modify.

The more important pattern is to use a template as a starting point or as a source of reusable pieces inside a larger app. Someone could turn a starter into an analytics app using the toolkit that was created by building the analytics app, adapt the workflow and instructions to their organization, connect its systems, or combine pieces from the Content, Slides, Analytics, and Design apps into an agent factory. The value is not that every customer needs to keep the template unchanged; it is that the framework and toolkit remove the need to invent the app structure and shared capabilities from scratch.

We do not yet have a mature catalog of public customer modifications to point to. The templates and apps are still being pressure-tested, and several of the apps have not been broadly announced or pushed yet.

Do we have proof of pain being felt right now?

The issue is not whether Claude can technically connect to MCPs. The repeated pain is that connections alone do not package the context, workflow, and guardrails needed to get reliable results for everyone on a team / in a company. Customers and prospects describe people using Claude with different configurations, different know-how, and different outcomes. We saw the same thing internally when people were told to use Claude projects and did not know what to set up or how to use them effectively.

For example, connecting BigQuery does not give an agent the organization’s data dictionary, approved example queries, dashboard conventions, or the workflow for deciding what to ask next. Those pieces need to be created, tested, shared, and maintained by the people who understand the domain. A focused analytics app can package that expertise and give users an interface with the right inputs, examples, outputs, and next steps.

Focused apps also avoid the context bloat and confusion of one super-agent that tries to do everything. They provide a structured path for repeatable work while preserving chat for anything outside the flow, and they can be accessed through the app, Slack, ChatGPT, APIs, or other agents. Engineering can own the underlying integrations and governance while subject-matter experts improve the workflows instead of every change becoming an engineering ticket.
Why would someone use AN in Builder rather than OS? Are there different use cases? What do we expect our customers to do?

Agent Native in Builder is how an organization becomes supercharged with agents. The goal is not to give every employee a blank chat box or ask engineering to build a custom agent for every workflow. It is to let anyone create, update, and share focused agents and agentic apps that make their own work faster and better.

Subject-matter experts can visually own and manage the workflows they understand best. Marketing can manage a content or assets agent, design can improve a brand agent, sales can refine a sales workflow, and operations can build an intake agent. They can add examples, adjust instructions, review outputs, and share improvements without turning every change into an engineering ticket or asking a non-SME engineer to guess how the work should be done. Engineering still owns the platform, integrations, guardrails, and production controls, but is no longer the bottleneck for every domain-specific improvement.

Customers should start with a high-value internal workflow, often from a template. Engineering sets the rails and controls production access, while the team that owns the work creates, improves, and shares the agent without turning every change into an engineering backlog item.

Yes. Clips could capture a user bug and ask Builder/Fusion to fix it and send a pull request to builder-internal. Agent-Native apps can talk to one another, and the A2A protocol also lets an app talk to another agent by URL.

Is factories an agent-native app or is it a broader concept within builder?

Factory is both a broad concept and an app. The concept is a repeatable workflow where apps or agents hand work to one another, and the Factory app helps create, visualize, run, and monitor that workflow.

A normal automation might be “every day, check Slack and do this” or “when a webhook fires, do that.” Factory is for a larger flow - for example, one agent produces something, another reviews it, and a third updates a system. It is a thin coordination layer, not a replacement for Zapier or n8n.
